header: Headlines from the news sites' own RSS feeds (the feeds they publish for exactly this use): a headline, where it came from, when, and the link to the story, which the card opens in a new tab. I take only the headline and the link, never the story: the reader goes to the publisher for it. This file is pure: the feed's text in, the items out (tested on saved slices of real feeds).

members.name: link
doc: An http(s) link to the story, nothing else; I drop a "javascript:" or "data:" link.

members.name: publishedAt
doc: ISO time, or "" when the feed gave none that could be read.

members.name: source
doc: The publisher, from the feed or, for an aggregator, the name after the last " - " of the headline.

members.name: summary
doc: The feed's own short description, tags removed. I use it only to sort sports stories and never show it.

members.name: also
doc: The other papers that carried the same story (the merge shows it once; these are the papers other than the one whose headline is shown).

members.name: id
doc: The story's own identity, which stays the same while papers add to it: the link of the first report. I key a card by it, so that a development rolls the card instead of adding a new one.

members.name: firstAt
doc: When, and by which paper, the story was first reported (the headline shown is the latest one; these say where it began).

members.name: desk
doc: The desk of the feed the item came from (a section of a paper: "sports", "metro"), set by the source; a story takes the desk of the paper of highest priority that carried it.

members.name: tier
doc: The rank of the story's desk on a curated tab (the Bengali one): 1 is the most important. The curation sets it, never a feed, and I never show it on a card.

symbols.name: NAMED
symbols.sig: const NAMED: Record<string, string> = { amp: "&", lt: "<", gt: ">", quot: '"', apos: "'", nbsp: " ", rsquo: "’", lsquo: "‘", rdquo: "”", ldquo: "“", hellip: " …

symbols.name: field
symbols.sig: function field(block: string, tag: string): string
doc: Returns the text of a tag: CDATA unwrapped, markup removed, entities decoded, white space collapsed.

symbols.name: parseRss
symbols.sig: export function parseRss(xml: string, defaultSource: string, splitSource = false): FeedItem[]
doc: Returns the items of an RSS 2.0 feed. `defaultSource` names the publisher when the item does not; with `splitSource`, a trailing " - Publisher" is moved out of the headline (Google News).

symbols.name: titleKey
doc: I compare the headlines of two feeds that are the same story by this key: lower case, only letters, marks (the vowel signs of Hindi and Bengali) and digits, the first 60 of them.

symbols.name: mergeFeeds
symbols.sig: export function mergeFeeds(feeds: FeedItem[][], limit: number, now: DateTime, maxAgeHours = 36, weights: number[] = []): FeedItem[]
doc: One list from several feeds, in the order of importance the feeds themselves give: the first story of each, then the second of each, and so on (a round robin; a feed of higher priority takes more places in each round, see the weights argument), so that no one publisher fills the list; I show the same story from several papers (even worded differently) once. Stories older than `maxAgeHours` are dropped when they carry a date.

One story, one card. The same event is worded differently by every paper, so I group stories by what they are about (sameStory), not by their exact headline. A story keeps the identity of its FIRST report (`id`, with `firstAt` and `firstSource`), and I show it by its LATEST headline, so that when a paper adds to the story the card's headline changes and the card does not move; the other papers are named (`also`). A story bridged by a third paper joins two groups into one, the earlier first report staying.

symbols.name: newestFirst
symbols.sig: export function newestFirst<T extends { publishedAt: string }>(items: T[], at: (i: T) => string = (i) => i.publishedAt): T[]
doc: Returns the stories newest first, as a wire shows them (a story with no time goes last, in the order it had). `at` says which time counts.

symbols.name: storyKey
symbols.sig: const storyKey = (i: { link: string; id?: string }): string =>
doc: A story's identity on the screen: the first report's link when the merge gave one, else its own link.

symbols.name: diffStories
symbols.sig: export function diffStories<T extends { link: string; id?: string }>(before: T[], after: T[]): { added: T[]; removed: T[]; changed: T[] }
symbols.returns: { added: T[]; removed: T[]; changed: T[] }
symbols.generics: T extends { link: string; id?: string }
doc: Tells what a refresh changed, by story identity: the stories that were not on the screen before (added), the ones that have left it (removed), and the ones that are still there but whose HEADLINE is now another paper's, later one (changed: a development). Order does not count.

symbols.name: FILLER
symbols.sig: const FILLER = new Set(("a an the and or but of in on at to for from by with as is are was were be been it its this that these those no …
doc: Words that every headline has and that tell nothing about WHICH story it is.

symbols.name: storyWords
doc: Returns the telling words of a headline: lower case, apostrophes dropped, a trailing plural s removed, filler left out, each word once. I let letters AND their combining marks make a word (Hindi and Bengali vowel signs).

symbols.name: wordCounts
symbols.sig: export function wordCounts(titles: string[]): Map<string, number>
doc: How common each telling word is across a batch of headlines: the number of headlines it is in.

symbols.name: DISTINCT_MAX
doc: I call a word DISTINCTIVE when few headlines of the batch use it: a name, a place, a figure; "Nvidia" in a week of Nvidia news is not, "Zakir" is.

symbols.name: SAME_SHARE
doc: The share of the shorter headline's weight that two headlines must have in common to be one story.

symbols.name: sameStory
symbols.sig: export function sameStory(a: string, b: string, counts?: Map<string, number>, total = 0): boolean
doc: Are these two headlines the same story? My rule: three things must hold, and a fourth must not:
- they share at least three telling words;

- at least TWO of the shared words are distinctive (few headlines of the batch use them), so that a week's running story ("Jensen Huang", "Nvidia", "CEO"), a section's template ("Roundup: Market Talk") or common words alone never make two different stories one;
- the shared words carry at least SAME_SHARE of the weight of the shorter headline, a word weighing more the fewer headlines use it;
- and they do NOT disagree on figures: if both have numbers and share none ("$65 billion", "$25 billion"), they are two stories with one template.
`counts` is the batch's wordCounts and `total` its number of headlines; without them every word weighs the same and every word counts as distinctive.

behaviours: The Hindu: four stories, CDATA unwrapped, link and source set
a +0530 date is read as the right instant (16:56 IST is 11:26 UTC)
Hindi headlines come through whole, with GMT dates
Bengali headlines: entities such as the curly quotes are decoded
an aggregator's ' - Publisher' is moved from the headline to the source
only <item> titles are read, not the channel's
only http(s) links are kept: javascript:, data: and nonsense are dropped
entities and dates
an item without a title or a link is left out
the merge is a round robin: the first story of each feed, then the second of each ...
the same story from two feeds is shown once, from the first
the limit holds, and stories older than 36 hours are dropped (a story with no date stays)
news from the feeds that answer, naming the ones that did not
when no feed answers, it is an error
three languages, each with feeds, and a whitelist of the language
each business feed gives its ten stories with a link on its own site and a time
Mint's and Business Line's CDATA links and dates are read; WSJ's GMT dates are read as GMT
WSJ's entities (— and ’) are decoded in the headlines
the business tab keeps 15 stories, shown by TIME, the latest at the top, like a wire (the time on the card is the order)
they are CHOSEN a paper at a time, so every one of the four is among the stories (none fills the screen alone), and no story is shown twice
a paper that does not answer is left out and named; the others still show
when none of the four answers, it is an error
the business sources are exactly the four free ones, each on its own https site; Business Standard and Financial Express are not asked (their servers refuse automated requests)
the tabs are Business first, then the three languages; the route accepts biz and the languages, nothing else
newest first; a story without a time goes last in its own order; ties keep their order
a refresh's difference is only arrivals and departures, by link: n1 came, c left
the same stories give no difference, whatever their order; an empty screen takes everything as new

the reader's own pair: The Hindu's 'Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off ... Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE' and Times of India's 'PM Modi inaugurates B'luru Metro Pink Line: Route, timings, cost ...' are one story

the same event in different words is one story (Zakir Naik ban from three papers, the Calcutta HC order, Delhi's air, SpaceX, Mexico tariffs, Wendy's, Jindal Power, the low-pressure area, Colette Kress, the derailment)

the running story is NOT one story: 'Jensen Huang Has Been Ousted' / 'A Timeline of the Scandals' / 'What we know after Jensen Huang resigns' / 'Why Jensen Huang resigned ...' are four different pieces

a section's template is not one story: 'Auto & Transport Roundup: Market Talk' and 'Health Care Roundup: Market Talk'; nor is one template with other figures: '$65 Billion' McCormick/Unilever and '$25 Billion' AkzoNobel/Axalta
two different things about one company are two stories (the words they share are only the company)
figures decide: the same words with different figures are two stories; the same figures with the same words are one
telling words: filler, months, years, plurals and apostrophes are left out
a hundred identical-template headlines do not make a story: the batch's common words do not count as distinctive
the real batch gives fewer rows than headlines (the duplicates are gone), and no kept row is a same-story of another kept row from a DIFFERENT paper

the Pink Line flag-off, which The Hindu, Times of India and Hindustan Times all carried, is ONE card: it began with Hindustan Times (its identity), shows the LATEST headline (The Hindu's) and names the other two
the Zakir Naik ban, which three papers carried, is one row naming the other two
a story has the IDENTITY of its first report and is shown by its LATEST headline: Early began it, Late's headline shows, and the card says where it began
when a third paper adds to the story the identity (so the card and its place) does not change, only the headline shown does
a story told by one paper only has itself as identity and no 'also'
a refresh's difference by story identity: A is CHANGED (a later headline, same story), L4 came, L3 left, L2 is untouched
a story a paper repeats itself is shown once but names no 'also' (that paper is the one shown)
Bengali and Hindi words are whole: 'সৌরভের' and 'পরিবর্তন' are one word each, not letters and fragments; the Devanagari 'प्रधानमंत्री' too
the same event worded alike in Bengali is one story; two different things about one person are not
Anandabazar through Google News: each headline has its paper split off ('Anandabazar Patrika') and a link on the way to the article
the printed edition's page listings ('... | রাজ্য - page 3') are told apart and left out; ordinary news and a plain 'page' word are not
the Bengali tab: Anandabazar is the FIRST source, its printed-page listings never reach the card, and it names itself
the Hindi tab is exactly the owner's five papers in his order: Dainik Bhaskar, Dainik Jagran, Amar Ujala, Hindustan, Navbharat Times; every address is https, none is BBC or an aggregator
each of the five Hindi feeds is read: ten (Amar Ujala eleven) dated Devanagari headlines with an https link on its own site
the Hindi tab: all five papers are used, in the owner's order, and none failed
the Hindi tab shows 15 stories and every paper has some of them
the one story that several Hindi papers carried (Rahul Gandhi's phone-tapping claim) is ONE card, not one per paper
the papers a card names are in the owner's order of priority, whatever the order they came in
the English tab is in the owner's order: The Telegraph, The Hindu, Times of India, Hindustan Times, The Indian Express, then NDTV and BBC News India
their PRIORITY is a weight: the top three are equal at 3 (the same level), Hindustan Times and The Indian Express equal at 2, the others 1
The Telegraph is read through Google News' public feed of telegraphindia.com (its own site refuses automated requests), its stories named 'The Telegraph' whatever Google calls it
Telegraph through Google: twelve headlines with ' - Telegraph India' taken off, each with a time and a link on the way to the article
The Indian Express's own free feed is read: ten dated headlines with an https link on indianexpress.com
every Telegraph story on the card is named 'The Telegraph' (not 'Telegraph India')
with the weights the first fifteen stories are 3 from each top paper, 2 from each second-rank paper, 1 from each of the rest: 3,3,3,2,2,1,1
equal weights are equal shares: the three top papers never get different numbers of stories

a story BELONGS to the paper of highest priority that carried it: first reported by a low-priority paper, carried later by a top one, it counts as the top paper's (named as 'first reported by' the other)
without weights the merge is the plain round robin as before (one from each in turn)
a paper whose list is short does not stop the others: the rest fill the places
sports: India is told from its words
sports: a world event with or without India, and a story may be both
Pakistan make U-19 Asia Cup final
the sports list is classified, and names the feeds that did not answer
the sports list is in TIME order, the latest at the top, though the papers are chosen by turns (Kohli 09:30 first, the 04:00 story last)
each sports tab (India, World events) is a filter of that one list, so it is in time order too
